title: "Study B (contraception) — quality control before analysis"
format: html
editor: source
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

> The point of a QC report is to find problems **before** they contaminate an
> analysis. Here we check the Study B data (93 participants on three
> contraceptives: pill, injectable, ring) for the boring-but-fatal issues:
> samples that don't line up between tables, missing values, samples with very
> few reads, and annotations that don't cover the features we will test.
>
> Each section works the same way: **what we're looking for** in plain words,
> then the code, then the figure, then **reading** — what we think it means.

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

source(here("R/count_tables.R"))
d <- read_counts("group_b")

meta  <- d$metadata
spec  <- d$species      # 220 species x 93 samples
genes <- d$genes        # 14,226 genes  x 93 samples
cyt   <- d$cytokines
```

# 1. The sample sheet

**What we're looking for.** The sample sheet is the row of truth: everything
else is matched to it. If it has duplicate samples or missing values, every
downstream join silently goes wrong. We also want to see the shape of the
groups — if one arm is much smaller, comparisons will be noisier there.

```{r}
# Shape, duplicate IDs, and missing cells
nrow(meta)
n_distinct(meta$sample_id) == nrow(meta)   # TRUE = no duplicates
sum(is.na(meta))                           # 0 = no missing values
```

```{r}
# Who is in each arm, and what do the clinical variables look like?
meta |> count(arm)
meta |> summarise(nugent_min = min(nugent), nugent_max = max(nugent),
                  ph_min = min(ph),         ph_max = max(ph))
meta |> count(bv)        # Nugent 0-3 negative, 7-10 positive (4-6 intermediate)
meta |> count(any_sti)
```

```{r}
# BV status across the three arms — each bar is one arm, all the same height
# (because the arms are unequal), so we compare the *proportions* within each.
ggplot(meta, aes(arm, fill = bv)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(negative = "#4DAF4A", intermediate = "#FFC107",
                               positive = "#E41A1C")) +
  labs(y = "fraction of participants", title = "BV status by arm")
```

**Reading.** 93 unique samples, nothing missing. The arms are unequal
(injectable has the most people) — that is normal in an observational
comparison and matters later for statistical power, not for QC. BV is common
in all three arms (39 positive), and the mix looks similar across arms, so
arm is not just a proxy for BV status.

# 2. Do all five tables describe the same 93 samples?

**What we're looking for.** The columns of both count tables must sit in
**exactly the metadata order**. DESeq2 matches columns to rows by position,
not by name — it will not warn if they disagree, it will just be wrong. (Our
loader reorders to match, but we check anyway.)

```{r}
# The sample_ids in metadata, and in each table's first row/column
count_cols <- function(m) colnames(m)

tibble(
  table = c("microbiome", "genes", "cytokines"),
  same_ids_as_metadata = c(
    identical(count_cols(spec),  meta$sample_id),
    identical(count_cols(genes), meta$sample_id),
    identical(cyt$sample_id,     meta$sample_id)
  )
)
```

**Reading.** All `TRUE` — every table is row-for-row aligned with the sample
sheet. There is no figure for this one because it's a yes/no: a single
`FALSE` here would stop everything until we fix it.

# 3. Sequencing depth (library size)

**What we're looking for.** The library size is how many reads landed in each
sample. A sample far below the others detected fewer things *because it was
sequenced less*, not because its biology differs — so we hunt for outliers.
The histogram shows the shape of the whole distribution; the bar chart of
samples sorted by depth makes individual outliers easy to name; and the
scatter checks whether the two sequencing runs (species and genes) agree
about which samples are shallow.

```{r}
# Total reads per sample, for both count tables
lib <- tibble(
  sample_id      = meta$sample_id,
  arm            = meta$arm,
  batch          = meta$rnaseq_batch,
  species_lib    = colSums(spec),
  gene_lib       = colSums(genes)
)

lib |> summarise(across(ends_with("lib"),
          list(min = min, median = median, max = max))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything())
```

```{r}
# Distribution of species depths. On a log scale, a healthy sample set looks
# like one broad lump; a broken sample sticks out as a lone bar far to the left.
ggplot(lib, aes(x = log10(species_lib))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25) +
  labs(x = "log10 species reads", title = "Distribution of species library sizes")
```

```{r}
# Species library sizes, smallest first; the red line is 10% of the median,
# a rough alarm bell for "too shallow to trust".
ggplot(arrange(lib, species_lib),
       aes(x = reorder(sample_id, species_lib), y = species_lib)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = median(lib$species_lib) / 10, colour = "red") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "sample", y = "species reads",
       title = "Species library sizes (line = 10% of median)")
```

```{r}
# The five shallowest species samples
lib |> slice_min(species_lib, n = 5) |>
  select(sample_id, arm, batch, species_lib)
```

```{r}
# Same picture for the gene table
ggplot(arrange(lib, gene_lib),
       aes(x = reorder(sample_id, gene_lib), y = gene_lib / 1e6)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "sample", y = "million gene reads",
       title = "Gene library sizes")
```

```{r}
# Do the two sequencing runs agree about which samples are shallow? If the
# shallowest species sample were fine on the gene side, the problem is
# sequencing, not the sample itself.
ggplot(lib, aes(species_lib, gene_lib / 1e6, colour = arm)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_point(data = filter(lib, species_lib == min(species_lib)),
             shape = 21, size = 5, stroke = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "species reads", y = "million gene reads",
       title = "Species vs gene depth per sample (circled = B006)")
```

**Reading.** Species depths run 5,247–77,357 with a median near 29,000. The
histogram shows one lump plus one lone bar far to the left — and the bar chart
names it: **B006**, 5,247 reads, roughly a sixth of the median. Gene depths
(5.9–24 million) are comfortably even; no gene sample needs attention. The
scatter shows B006 is not unusually shallow for genes, so this is likely a
low-yield bacterial extraction rather than a bad sample. **Decision:** drop
B006 from downstream species analyses or keep it and check it isn't driving
results — a choice to record.

# 4. Sparsity and dominance

**What we're looking for.** Both tables are **compositional**: sequencing
gives proportions, not absolute amounts. We look at (a) how sparse each table
is, (b) how common each feature is — a species seen in only 2 samples is noise
we can't test, and (c) how much one feature can dominate a sample, because
that shapes what transformations are legal later.

```{r}
# Fraction of zeros, and the biggest share any single feature holds in a sample
rel_max <- function(m) apply(sweep(m, 2, colSums(m), "/"), 2, max)

tibble(
  table          = c("species", "genes"),
  n_features     = c(nrow(spec), nrow(genes)),
  frac_zeros     = c(mean(spec == 0), mean(genes == 0)),
  median_rel     = c(median(rel_max(spec)), median(rel_max(genes))),
  max_rel        = c(max(rel_max(spec)),    max(rel_max(genes)))
)
```

```{r}
# Prevalence: in how many samples is each species detected? A species seen in
# 1-2 samples is noise we can't test; the bar chart shows how many are common.
prev <- rowSums(spec > 0)
ggplot(tibble(n_samples = prev), aes(x = n_samples)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(x = "number of samples (out of 93) in which the species is detected",
       y = "number of species", title = "Species prevalence")
```

```{r}
# Rank-abundance curve for a typical sample: sort its species from most to
# least abundant and plot. A steep fall = one species dominates; a long flat
# tail = many rare species. The typical sample is the one closest to the
# median library size.
typical_id <- lib$sample_id[which.min(abs(lib$species_lib - median(lib$species_lib)))]
x <- sort(spec[, typical_id], decreasing = TRUE)
x <- x[x > 0]
ggplot(tibble(rank = seq_along(x), abundance = x),
       aes(rank, abundance)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "rank (1 = most abundant)", y = "reads",
       title = str_glue("Rank-abundance curve, sample {typical_id} (median depth)"))
```

**Reading.** The species table is very sparse (~88% zeros — each sample sees
only a subset of the 220 species). The prevalence histogram is the classic
microbiome shape: most species are detected in only a handful of samples, a
few are detected in nearly all. The steep rank-abundance curve means one
*Lactobacillus* often exceeds half the reads. The gene table is dense (~3%
zeros). Sparsity pushes us toward composition-aware methods (CLR, DESeq2) for
the species table; the gene table can take the usual RNA-seq pipeline. When we
filter later, a prevalence threshold (e.g. species seen in ≥10% of samples)
will drop the long tail of singletons.

# 5. Are these really counts?

**What we're looking for.** Raw counts must be whole, non-negative numbers
with no missings, or DESeq2 refuses / misbehaves. This is a pass/fail check —
no figure needed. If it fails, the "fix" is usually to go back to the
exporter, not to patch the numbers here.

```{r}
stopifnot(
  all(spec  >= 0), all(genes >= 0),
  all(spec  == round(spec)), all(genes == round(genes)),
  !any(is.na(spec)), !any(is.na(genes))
)
"count tables: all checks passed"
```

```{r}
# Cytokines are allowed to have gaps — but we need to know where they are
sum(is.na(cyt))
cyt_nas <- cyt |>
  filter(if_any(-sample_id, is.na)) |>
  pull(sample_id)
cyt_nas
```

**Reading.** Both count tables pass. Two participants, **B018 and B029, are
missing every cytokine value** — presumably the assay failed for their
samples, not individual markers. Consequence: cytokine analyses run on 91
samples, and the count-table analyses on all 93, so the two arms of the
project rest on slightly different sample sets. Worth saying so in any report
that joins the tables.

# 6. Do the features have names we can interpret?

**What we're looking for.** If a taxon or gene lacks annotation we can measure
it but not explain it. We also want to know what kinds of features are in the
gene table — a gene list dominated by pseudogenes or NAs would change what
"enrichment" means later.

```{r}
# Every counted taxon/gene should have exactly one annotation row
taxa_ok  <- setequal(rownames(spec), d$taxonomy$taxon)
genes_ok <- setequal(rownames(genes), d$gene_info$ensembl_gene_id)
taxa_ok; genes_ok
```

```{r}
# Gene annotation categories, and duplicate symbols
d$gene_info |> count(locus_group, sort = TRUE)

d$gene_info |>
  count(symbol) |>
  filter(n > 1)
```

```{r}
# The annotation categories, as a picture
ggplot(d$gene_info, aes(x = fct_reorder(locus_group, locus_group, .fun = length))) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "number of genes",
       title = "Gene annotation categories")
```

**Reading.** Full annotation coverage in both tables — every counted feature
has exactly one row. One catch for later: two different Ensembl genes share a
symbol, so any per-symbol aggregation (that includes
`tax_transform(rank = "symbol")` in microViz) will merge their counts. Gene-level
analyses are unaffected.

# 7. Cytokines

**What we're looking for.** Cytokines are measured in pg/mL, usually on a log
scale. We want to see (a) the range of each cytokine, (b) which ones sit at
suspiciously exact repeated minima — a sign of the assay's **lower limit of
detection** (LLOD) rather than true measurements — and (c) the outliers.

```{r}
# Range of each cytokine, sorted by the smallest value measured
cyt |>
  summarise(across(-sample_id, list(min = min, max = max))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("cytokine", "stat"),
               names_pattern = "(.*)_(min|max)") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = stat, values_from = value) |>
  arrange(min)
```

```{r}
# All cytokines on one log-scale plot. Cytokines vary over orders of
# magnitude, so the log scale is the honest one. Everything crammed along
# one flat line at the bottom of its box is the same story: the LLOD floor.
cyt_long <- cyt |> pivot_longer(-sample_id, names_to = "cytokine", values_to = "pg_ml")
ggplot(cyt_long, aes(cytokine, pg_ml)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "pg/mL (log scale)", title = "Cytokine distributions")
```

```{r}
# The minimum value of each cytokine — the values that repeat exactly
# (e.g. 0.005) are the LLOD floor, not real measurements.
cyt_long |>
  group_by(cytokine) |>
  summarise(min_value = min(pg_ml, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(cytokine, min_value)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "minimum measured pg/mL (log scale)",
       title = "Minimum values — the LLOD floors")
```

**Reading.** No missing values except B018 and B029 (see section 5). Several
cytokines have minimum values that repeat suspiciously exactly (e.g. 0.005
pg/mL) — almost certainly the assay's **lower limit of detection** rather than
true measurements. If we model those cytokines we should treat sub-LLOD values
carefully (e.g. censor or log after adding a small constant), not take 0.005
literally.

# 8. Batch effects

**What we're looking for.** RNA-seq was run in two batches (B1, B2). A batch
effect is only dangerous if it is tangled with the grouping variable: if
every pill sample were in batch B1 and every ring sample in B2, "arm" and
"batch" would be the same thing and we couldn't tell them apart. The grid
shows whether the two cross; the density plot shows whether the two batches
produce systematically different depths.

```{r}
table(meta$rnaseq_batch, meta$arm)   # rows = batch, cols = arm
```

```{r}
# Gene library size by batch — a crude look for a level shift
ggplot(lib, aes(batch, gene_lib / 1e6)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(y = "million gene reads")
```

```{r}
# The full distribution of gene depths per batch, overlaid: if the two curves
# sat on top of each other, the batches are interchangeable. Peaks in the
# same place, similar spread — that is what we see.
ggplot(lib, aes(gene_lib / 1e6, colour = batch)) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "million gene reads", y = "density",
       title = "Gene library size by batch")
```

**Reading.** Both arms appear in both batches at similar numbers (pill 14/14,
injectable 20/19, ring 13/13), so batch and arm are not confounded. The
density curves overlap almost completely. We still keep `rnaseq_batch` in
mind as a covariate for the differential-expression step, which is standard
practice.

# Verdict

| Check | Result | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Sample sheet complete, unique, no gaps | pass | — |
| Tables aligned to metadata order | pass | — |
| Species depth | one low sample (B006) | decide drop vs keep before species analyses |
| Gene depth | even | — |
| Counts integer, non-negative, no NA | pass | — |
| Annotations | complete; 1 shared symbol | aggregate per gene ID, not symbol |
| Cytokines | B018, B029 all-NA; sub-LLOD floors | cytokine analyses on 91 samples; handle LLOD |
| Batch vs arm | not confounded | adjust for batch in DE models |

Nothing here blocks the analysis. The one real decision is what to do with
B006 in species-table work.

**To check our numbers yourself:**
- `colSums(spec)[order(colSums(spec))[1:5]]` should print B006 at 5,247 on top.
- `rowSums(is.na(cyt))` should print two samples with 15 missing values each
  (B018 and B029) and 91 with none.
- `table(meta$rnaseq_batch, meta$arm)` should reproduce the 2×3 grid above.

# Choices made

- Low-depth alarm line: 10% of the median library size — alternatives were a fixed 1,000-read floor or interquartile-range outlier rules.
- B006 flagged, not dropped here — dropping is a per-analysis decision recorded in each report.
- Sparsity judged by fraction of zeros, prevalence, and maximum single-feature share — alternatives were Shannon diversity or prevalence filtering (deferred to the analysis reports).
- Rank-abundance curve shown for one median-depth sample — a single representative, not a full colour-by-arm grid.
- Batch assessed by tabulation, library-size boxplot, and density curves — no formal ordination coloured by batch yet, which the community report can add.
- Sub-LLOD cytokines described, not corrected — correction method belongs to whichever report models them.
